programmeChallenge: Actual Pharmacology studies molecular/wholebody action,PKPD,metabolism,toxicity,targetidentification andquantitative virtualexperiments. MolecularCellBiology includes a drug-target/action/metabolism/adverseeffects primaryliterature paper/poster. These, with diseasegenetics,biochemistry,physiology andlaboratorymethods, materiallyrespond to the biological/evaluation pillar of the target, not just a generic coherent science curriculum. Chemistry/design/delivery remains a major gap explicitly shown. Quantitative route retains this biological drug-action core and prioritises optimisation,neuralprediction,calculus anddynamics, corroborated by compulsorymodelling/ML andoptionalcomputational direction. No drug-specific application is fabricated for generic math/AI courses.

course.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
course.name: Personal & Professional Development
course.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
course.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
course.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

selected.contribution: Required Year1 PPD

course.description2: Covers computational methods for search problems in complex and adversarial environments. Includes uninformed and informed search, local and global search, adversarial games and constraint satisfaction problems.
course.name: Optimization Methods in AI
course.profile: Studies search and optimization for rational agents in known, complex and adversarial environments. Students move from uninformed and heuristic search to local and global optimization, first- and second-order methods and population approaches. Adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimization extend the toolkit. Laboratories and projects require algorithm tracing, implementation and evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.
course.discipline: Artificial intelligence; Mathematical optimization; Computer science
course.topics: Intelligent and rational agents; Uninformed and informed search; Heuristic functions; Search in complex environments; Local and global optimization; First- and second-order optimization; Population methods; Adversarial games; Constraint satisfaction; Linear programming; Discrete optimization
course.methods: Uninformed and heuristic search; Local and global search; First- and second-order optimization; Population-based optimization; Adversarial search; Monte Carlo tree search; Constraint-satisfaction algorithms; Linear programming; Discrete optimization; Algorithm implementation and experimental evaluation

selected.contribution: Complementary search, gradient and population optimisation, constraint solving and algorithm evaluation develop computational tools relevant to fitting and optimising models. The taught applications concern intelligent systems rather than drug design.

course.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
course.name: Introduction to Data Science
course.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
course.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
course.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

selected.contribution: Direct data cleaning, visualisation, R programming and project-based analysis provide the data-handling methods needed in biomedical research; actual UCR datasets span fields, not specifically drug research.

course.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
course.name: Machine Learning
course.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
course.discipline: Machine learning; Statistical learning; Data science
course.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
course.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

selected.contribution: Direct regression, classification, resampling and clustering provide the statistical-learning methods evidenced in the external computational curriculum; pharmaceutical training datasets are not claimed.

course.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
course.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
course.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
course.discipline: Machine learning; Deep learning; Data science
course.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
course.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design

selected.contribution: Complementary neural-network construction, backpropagation, validation and Python implementation supply advanced predictive methods for the target’s evidenced computational drug-research direction. Actual UCR projects use tabular, image or text data; pharmaceutical datasets are not promised.

course.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
course.name: Introduction to Programming
course.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
course.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
course.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

selected.contribution: Direct structured and object-oriented Python programming, testing and computational problem-solving provide an implementation foundation for reproducible biomedical-data and modelling workflows.

course.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
course.name: Mathematical Methods
course.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
course.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
course.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

selected.contribution: Direct calculus and differential equations plus a dynamic-model project provide mathematical methods supporting biological concentration/response models; UCR projects are general scientific models.

course.description2: Introduces systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces with emphasis on visual and conceptual understanding. Applies concepts across fields and includes hands‑on exercises using computer algebra software.
course.name: Linear Algebra
course.profile: Develops linear algebra from systems of equations and matrix operations to vector spaces, linear transformations, eigenvalues and orthogonality. Students study least-squares approximation, symmetric matrices, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis. Mathematica exercises teach computer-algebra approaches to larger problems alongside analytical problem-solving.
course.topics: Linear systems and matrix algebra; Linear independence, span, basis, dimension and rank; Linear transformations; Determinants and invertibility; Vector spaces; Eigenvalues and eigenvectors; Difference equations and Markov chains; Discrete signals and Fourier series; Orthogonality and inner products; Quadratic forms and constrained optimization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis
course.methods: Row reduction; Matrix factorization and diagonalization; Change of basis; Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization; Orthogonal projection; Least-squares fitting and QR factorization; Singular value decomposition; Principal component analysis; Mathematica computer-algebra computation

selected.contribution: Complementary matrix, vector, eigenvalue and least-squares methods develop the linear-algebra tools used in multivariable models and predictive data analysis; biological applications are a programme-level connection.

course.description2: Introduces numerical methods such as root‑finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration and solving differential equations. Emphasises algorithm accuracy, stability and efficiency and uses computer algebra software.
course.name: Computational & Numerical Methods
course.profile: Develops numerical solutions to mathematical problems that lack convenient analytical solutions, emphasizing when algorithms work and how to validate their output. Students study numerical root finding, interpolation, differentiation, quadrature, ordinary differential equations, and linear and nonlinear systems. Mathematica notebooks apply and compare textbook algorithms with built-in routines, with attention to roundoff, convergence, error, stability and sensitivity.
course.discipline: Numerical analysis; Computational mathematics; Scientific computing
course.topics: Computer arithmetic and roundoff; Algorithm convergence and error; Scalar root finding; Polynomial interpolation and splines; Parametric curves; Numerical differentiation and integration; Initial-value problems; Multistep and adaptive differential-equation methods; Stability and stiff equations; Linear systems and matrix factorization; Nonlinear systems; Numerical-result validation
course.methods: Mathematica numerical computation; Bisection, fixed-point, Newton and secant methods; Polynomial and spline interpolation; Numerical differentiation and Richardson extrapolation; Simpson, Romberg and Gaussian quadrature; Adaptive quadrature; Euler and Runge-Kutta methods; Multistep predictor-corrector methods; Gaussian elimination and pivoting; Matrix factorizations; Newton and quasi-Newton methods for systems; Steepest descent; Continuation methods

selected.contribution: Complementary numerical root finding, integration and differential-equation solvers develop computational tools for dynamic modelling. UCR teaches general numerical problems, not population PKPD simulation.

course.description2: Extends elementary calculus to multiple dimensions and differential equations, including complex‑valued functions. Uses computer algebra software to deepen analytical skills for science and data analysis applications.
course.name: Advanced Calculus

selected.contribution: Complementary multidimensional calculus and differential equations extend the analytical tools for quantitative biological modelling; no detailed pharmaceutical method beyond the description is claimed.

course.description2: Focuses on analysis of linear systems from an engineering perspective. Explores representations via differential equations, transfer functions, state‑space and signal‑flow diagrams and discusses applications in control, signal processing and modelling.
course.name: Linear Systems
course.profile: Analyzes continuous- and discrete-time signals and linear time-invariant systems through differential or difference equations, impulse responses and frequency-domain representations. Convolution, Fourier series and transforms lead into sampling and reconstruction, filtering, communication systems, Laplace and Z-transforms, and linear feedback. Mathematica laboratories and an applied project connect mathematical properties to signal processing and system behaviour.
course.discipline: Applied mathematics; Signal processing; Systems and control
course.topics: Continuous- and discrete-time signals; System linearity, causality and stability; Impulse and frequency responses; Convolution; Fourier series and transforms; Time-frequency representations; Sampling, reconstruction and aliasing; Digital filtering; Modulation and multiplexing; Laplace and Z-transforms; Regions of convergence and pole-zero representations; Linear feedback and stability
course.methods: Convolution sums and integrals; Fourier-series and Fourier-transform analysis; Bode-plot analysis; Sampling and signal reconstruction; Filter analysis; Modulation and demodulation; Laplace and Z-transform analysis; Block-diagram system analysis; Root-locus analysis; Mathematica signal and system computation

selected.contribution: Complementary differential/difference equations, impulse responses, transforms and feedback give mathematical tools for time-dependent responses and dynamical modelling. The course applies these to signals and systems; it is not pharmacometrics.

course.description2: Provides a foundation in mathematical statistics. Covers probability theory, discrete and continuous distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and simulation; uses computer algebra software to develop theoretical understanding and practical skills.
course.name: Probability & Statistics
course.profile: Provides a rigorous introduction to probability and mathematical statistics, from probability spaces and random variables to multivariate distributions and statistical inference. Students study estimation, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and maximum-likelihood methods, followed by an introduction to Bayesian reasoning. Mathematica simulations verify analytical results. A substantial project implements and compares random-sampling algorithms, including inverse sampling, accept-reject sampling and Gibbs sampling.
course.topics: Probability spaces and conditional probability; Random variables and expectation; Moment-generating functions; Discrete and continuous distributions; Multivariate and conditional distributions; Transformations and correlation; Sampling and order statistics; Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; Estimation efficiency; Bayesian inference; Monte Carlo methods
course.methods: Analytical probability calculation; Maximum-likelihood estimation and testing; Chi-square tests; Bootstrap; EM algorithm; Bayesian updating; Inverse-transform sampling; Accept-reject sampling; Gibbs sampling; Monte Carlo simulation in Mathematica

selected.contribution: Direct probability, estimation, hypothesis testing and simulation supply the uncertainty and inference methods needed in biomedical measurement; the UCR course emphasises mathematical statistics.

course.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
course.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
course.profile: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
course.topics: Disease frequency and risk; Incidence and prevalence; Measures of association; Epidemiological study designs; Bias, confounding and causality; Outbreak investigation; Social and environmental health determinants; Health inequalities; Health promotion; Health-needs assessment; Screening; Evidence-informed interventions and implementation
course.methods: Epidemiological rate and risk calculation; Descriptive and analytic epidemiology; Study-design and evidence appraisal; Population-health data interpretation; Outbreak analysis; Health-needs assessment; Stakeholder interviewing; Evidence-informed intervention development

selected.contribution: Direct epidemiological research designs, bias, confounding, risk measures and intervention appraisal support the pharmacoepidemiological strand of drug development and safety evaluation; UCR applications concern public health.

course.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
course.name: Functional Anatomy
course.profile: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Skeletal, thoracic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, reproductive and lower urinary anatomy are developed through spatial reasoning, medical images, anatomical drawing and human-specimen material. Guided practicals and dissection-room observation connect three-dimensional relationships to variation. Historical, ethical and societal questions about human remains, representation and sex accompany the anatomical study; activities are framed as academic learning rather than clinical qualification.
course.discipline: Human anatomy; Functional anatomy; Biomedical ethics
course.topics: Anatomical terminology and body planes; Medical imaging; Skeletal system and vertebral column; Thorax and pelvis; Respiratory and cardiovascular systems; Abdominal organs and vascular supply; Reproductive and lower urinary systems; Anatomical variation and intersex presentations; Human remains and dissection ethics; History and representation of the body
course.methods: Surface-anatomy observation; Anatomical image interpretation; Scientific anatomical drawing; Three-dimensional anatomical reasoning; Guided study of human skeletal remains and anatomical specimens; Ethical reflection on anatomical practice

selected.contribution: connects anatomical structure with organ-system function and medical imaging, locating drug action and disease effects within the human body

course.description2: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
course.name: Pharmacology
course.profile: Studies how drugs act at molecular, cellular and whole-body levels and how the body handles them. Pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, metabolism, toxicity and pharmacogenomics provide foundations for rational therapies and drug-target identification. Applications emphasize nervous-system drugs, antimicrobial treatment and inflammatory, immune and airway conditions. Quantitative exercises and virtual experiments model drug responses, while a psychoactive-drug project proposes a testable follow-up experiment.
course.topics: Drug discovery and targets; Drug-receptor interactions; Pharmacodynamics; Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination; Pharmacokinetics; Antimicrobial therapy; Inflammation and immunopharmacology; Autonomic regulation; Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Pharmacogenomics; Drug toxicity; Access to experimental treatments and evidence; Homeopathy
course.methods: Concentration-response modelling; Pharmacokinetic time-concentration and time-response analysis; Pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic parameter calculation; Virtual organ-bath experiments; Hypothesis and experimental-design development

selected.contribution: directly studies drug targets, molecular interactions, pharmacokinetics, toxicity and quantitative concentration-response relationships

course.description2: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
course.name: Infection & Immunity
course.profile: Examines host-microbe interactions and the immune mechanisms that protect against infection or cause disease. Microbiology and innate defence lead into antibodies, antigen recognition, lymphocyte development and memory, effector responses and mucosal immunity. Vaccination, allergy, immunodeficiency and autoimmunity connect mechanisms to clinical problems. Students analyze lymphocyte phenotypes using original flow-cytometry data and synthesize recent research in an extended and graphical abstract.
course.topics: Infectious agents and microbial virulence; Host defence and immune evasion; Immune cells, organs and cytokines; Innate immunity and complement; Antibodies and antigen recognition; MHC and lymphocyte receptors; Lymphocyte activation, development and memory; Cell- and antibody-mediated immunity; Mucosal immunity; Vaccination and viral infections; Hypersensitivity and allergy; Immunodeficiency; Autoimmune disease; Outbreak management
course.methods: Flow-cytometry data analysis and lymphocyte phenotyping; Clinical symptom and mechanism analysis; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Critical analysis of immunological research; Graphical synthesis of scientific findings

selected.contribution: studies immune recognition, host-pathogen interactions and immunopathology as disease mechanisms and therapeutic targets

course.description2: Examines molecular and cellular defects triggering pathologies. Presents clinical cases, discusses disease mechanisms and treatments across systems and includes an assignment to invent an imaginary disease.
course.name: Mechanisms of Disease
course.profile: Connects normal organ function to pathophysiology across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Students integrate anatomy and physiology to explain symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnostic findings, treatment and prognosis. Published clinical cases develop differential reasoning and appraisal of diagnostic procedures. A creative assignment constructs an imaginary disease whose symptoms, mechanism and proposed treatment must form a coherent pathophysiological account.
course.topics: Organ-system disease mechanisms; Nutrition and digestive disease; Hematological and cardiovascular disease; Respiratory disease; Renal failure, dialysis and transplantation; Endocrine disorders; Neurological disease; Etiology and pathogenesis; Diagnosis, treatment and prognosis; Medical ethics; Rheumatic disease
course.methods: Clinical case analysis; Differential diagnosis reasoning; Critical appraisal of diagnostic and laboratory procedures; Integration of anatomy, physiology and clinical evidence; Mechanistic modelling of an imaginary disease; Biomedical literature comparison

selected.contribution: derives pathophysiology across organ systems from anatomy and physiology, providing the disease-mechanism basis for rational intervention

course.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
course.name: Neurobiology
course.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
course.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
course.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders

selected.contribution: Complementary nervous-system anatomy, regulatory behaviour, research models and lifestyle-drug effects deepen the biological context for neuroactive therapies; animal-research welfare is considered.

course.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
course.name: Perception & Action

selected.contribution: Complementary study of sensory processing and goal-directed action develops the neural-system context for nervous-system drug actions. No pharmaceutical or experimental method beyond the course description is asserted.

course.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
course.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
course.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
course.discipline: Cell biology; Molecular biology; Biochemistry; Biomedical science
course.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
course.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments

selected.contribution: Direct biological molecules, DNA, cells, membranes, signalling and metabolism establish the molecular and cellular foundation for pharmacology and disease study.

course.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
course.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
course.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
course.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
course.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis

selected.contribution: introduces brain and behavioural science plus experimental methods as the formal foundation for later treatment-evidence synthesis and neural applications

course.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
course.name: Molecular Cell Biology
course.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
course.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
course.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis

selected.contribution: studies cellular structure, signalling, gene regulation and drug mechanisms, directly connecting molecular biology with therapeutic action

course.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
course.name: Human Physiology
course.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
course.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
course.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision

selected.contribution: studies homeostasis, signalling and integrated organ-system physiology needed to understand drug effects in the human body

course.description2: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
course.name: Biochemistry
course.profile: Examines the chemistry of life, emphasizing biomolecular structure and function, enzymes and metabolic pathways. Students study proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, enzyme kinetics and regulation, glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, the citric-acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation and further carbohydrate, lipid and nitrogen metabolism. Protein-biochemistry techniques are discussed. A literature-based disease project links a biochemical defect to symptoms, diagnostics and treatment, keeping the molecular mechanism central.
course.topics: Water and weak bonds; Amino acids and protein structure; Protein-biochemistry techniques; Enzyme action, kinetics, regulation and inhibition; Hemoglobin; Carbohydrates and lipids; Metabolic organization; Glycolysis and gluconeogenesis; Citric-acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation; Glycogen and pentose-phosphate metabolism; Fatty-acid and lipid metabolism; Nitrogen and urea cycle; Biochemical mechanisms of disease
course.methods: Biochemical pathway and disease-mechanism analysis; Primary-literature review

selected.contribution: studies biomolecule chemistry, metabolism and molecular dysfunction, supplying the biochemical foundation while not replacing organic or medicinal chemistry

course.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
course.name: Life Science Laboratory
course.profile: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
course.discipline: Molecular biology; Biochemistry; Microbiology; Laboratory life sciences; Bioinformatics
course.topics: Blood cells and proteins; Blood groups and hemograms; Aseptic culture and bacterial identification; Disinfection and sterilization; Antibiotic susceptibility; Genetically modified bacteria; GFP production and purification; DNA and plasmid analysis; PCR and restriction digestion; Protein and DNA databases; Genotype and population-genetic interpretation; Experimental reproducibility
course.methods: Pipetting and workflow planning; Microscopy and blood-smear examination; Blood cell counting and hemogram measurement; ELISA; Aseptic culture and purity streaking; Bacterial identification and inhibition-zone testing; Sterilization and disinfection testing; pGLO bacterial transformation; Protein extraction and chromatographic purification; SDS-PAGE; DNA and plasmid isolation; PCR; Restriction digestion and agarose-gel electrophoresis; DNA and protein database searching; Laboratory notebook and scientific-report preparation

selected.contribution: Direct biochemical, microbial and molecular laboratory training, including bacterial transformation, fluorescent protein purification and DNA analysis, supplies practical experimental skills. It does not establish organic synthesis or a completed independent pharmaceutical experiment.

course.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
course.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
course.profile: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
course.discipline: Molecular pathology; Human genetics; Molecular medicine
course.topics: Cell injury, adaptation and death; Acute and chronic inflammation; Regeneration, repair and fibrosis; Neoplasia; Pulmonary pathology; Leukemia and lymphoma; Genes, genomes and inheritance; Genetic variation and chromosome abnormalities; Gene regulation and epigenetics; Genotype-phenotype relationships; Genetic testing and DNA technologies; Gene-based therapies and cell manipulation; Genetics ethics, law and biosafety
course.methods: Biomedical literature review; Research-grant proposal design; Hypothesis formulation and experimental-control selection; Research feasibility, timeline and budget planning; Stakeholder-based ethical argument analysis

selected.contribution: studies molecular pathology, genetic disease, testing and treatment as mechanisms linking biological discovery to intervention

course.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
course.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
course.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
course.discipline: Applied statistics; Behavioural research methods; Health research methods

course.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
course.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
course.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.

course.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting

distinctness.finding: Four courses / 30 EC differ in each direction. Functional Anatomy, Infection & Immunity, Neurobiology and Perception & Action are replaced by Advanced Calculus, Linear Systems, Optimisation Methods in AI and Neural Networks & Deep Learning. This is a substantive shift from biological-system applications to quantitative therapeutic modelling, not threshold-filling substitution.

stopping.assessment: Two complete related-field programmes pass evidence, course-content, schedule and 30-EC distinctness gates. A third medicinal-chemistry and targeted-delivery route is not defensible because the workbook lacks general and organic chemistry sequences, medicinal chemistry, analytical pharmaceutical chemistry, synthesis, formulation, drug-delivery technology and chemistry laboratories. Molecular biology and biochemistry are not relabelled as those missing subjects.

progression: All 24 unique courses total 180 EC, with four per semester, Year-1 PPD and 6 advanced courses. Every formal prerequisite is completed earlier and every actual assigned-term offering checked against the current workbook. Physiology and biochemistry precede Pharmacology; programming, data science and Mathematical Methods precede advanced computational work. Molecular Cell Biology and evidence synthesis precede final-year computational projects in the quantitative programme. No additional hard prerequisite is inferred from course level.
